texts.city: Two incomes of $280,000 and $511,000 net worth but vulnerable due to thin cash and large protection shortfalls.
texts.strength: You save $26,000 a year and hold $330,000 in investable assets to build from.

cashflow.building: Free cash flow is small: $15,032 a year.
cashflow.plain: After taxes, bills and savings you have $15,032 a year left. Think of it as the monthly leftovers you split between goals.
cashflow.standard: Net cash flow this year is $15,032 a year and income is $280,000. Yearly savings total $26,000 a year and current savings go to the 529 ($8,000) and a taxable account ($12,000). Closing your retirement gap is projected to need $34,165 a year, which is more than twice your free cash flow.

cushion.building: Accessible cash is $19,000, far below the 8–9 month target.
cushion.plain: You have $19,000 available today, which covers only a little over a month of essentials. It’s like having a small spare tire when you need a full-size one.
cushion.standard: Accessible cash (bank plus money market) is $19,000 and covers 1.4 months of essential expenses. Recommended emergency reserve is $106,860 to $120,218, leaving an $87,860 shortfall; with the $4,500 vacation set aside the shortfall grows to $92,360 and coverage drops to 1.1 months.

retirement.building: Nothing is going into retirement today; a $1,427,456 retirement-account gap exists.
retirement.plain: Your plan projects retirement spending need of $124,071 a year. Social Security covers about half; savings must cover the rest.
retirement.standard: Yearly retirement spending need is $124,071 a year, with guaranteed income of $59,466 a year covering 49% of that need. Yearly retirement spending to be paid from savings is $62,932 a year, and the retirement-account gap at retirement is $1,427,456; extra yearly savings projected to close the gap are $34,165 a year.

debt.building: Total debt is $618,000, with a high-rate card of $18,000 at 24.9%.
debt.plain: You owe $618,000 in total, most of it a mortgage. One credit card charges much higher interest than the rest.
debt.standard: Total debt is $618,000 (220.71% of income) with a $560,000 mortgage at 6.5%. The Chase Sapphire card is $18,000 at 24.9% and paid $450 a month, projected to be paid off by January 2034 if that payment continues. Housing and debt payments are 27.25% of income.

protection.building: Life cover is well below recommended levels and no umbrella is in place.
protection.plain: Daniel has $250,000 life insurance; Emily has $200,000. Recommended ranges are much higher, and you have no umbrella policy.
protection.standard: Daniel’s life insurance is $250,000 against a recommended $1,600,000 to $2,400,000; Emily’s is $200,000 against $1,200,000 to $1,800,000, leaving shortfalls of $1,350,000 and $1,000,000 respectively. Umbrella liability cover: None, with a recommended $1,000,000.

college.building: College gap is $106,552 despite $30,000 saved in 529s and $8,000 yearly contributions.
college.plain: You have $30,000 in 529 accounts and add $8,000 a year, but still face a remaining need. Think of the 529 as a partially filled college jar.
college.standard: Saved in 529 accounts: $30,000 with $8,000 a year going in. Still to fund for college total $106,552 today: Oliver needs $50,742 (starts August 2033) and Sophia $55,810 (starts August 2035).

investments.building: Investable assets $330,000, but portfolio stock allocation is below target.
investments.plain: You hold $330,000 of invested savings and $250,000 in 401(k)s, but contributions are $0 today. Your portfolio has more cash and bonds than the plan target.
investments.standard: Total assets include $750,000 home and $330,000 invested savings. Two 401(k)s hold $250,000 combined ($150,000 Daniel, $100,000 Emily) with no contributions today. Your mix today is 54% stocks, 36% bonds, 10% cash versus a target of 66% stocks, 27% bonds, 6% cash.

score.building: Overall score 52/100 in the vulnerable band, weakest in insurance and protection.
score.plain: Your published score is 52, which the plan calls vulnerable. Insurance and protection score 0/20, pulling the total down.
score.standard: The published score is 52. Strengths include liquidity (13/15 points) while insurance and protection are 0/20. The plan’s top move is adding $1,166,000 of life cover to reach the next mortality-coverage anchor and raise the score from 52 to 57.

assumptions.building: Plan assumptions set retirement ages, growth rates and future incomes.
assumptions.plain: The plan assumes Daniel retires at 62 and Emily at 60, with prices rising 3% a year. Investments are assumed to grow 7.58% a year.
assumptions.standard: Key assumptions: Daniel retires at 62 and Emily at 60, plan runs to age 91, prices rise 3% a year, investments grow 7.58% a year, Daniel’s salary $160,000 and Emily’s $120,000 continue until 2044, and Social Security starts for Daniel in 2049 and Emily in 2051.

m0.title: Add life coverage
m0.why: The plan shows large life-insurance shortfalls: Daniel $1,350,000 and Emily $1,000,000.
steps: List current life policies and their death benefits and beneficiaries
Calculate how much more each of you needs versus recommended range
Get quotes from your insurer or agent for the additional cover
Decide together how much of the $1,166,000 addition to buy now

quiz.q: According to the plan, how much life cover is Daniel short by?
quiz.explain: The plan lists Daniel’s shortfall as $1,350,000 versus the recommended $1,600,000 to $2,400,000.

m1.title: Buy an umbrella policy
m1.why: You have no umbrella cover while the plan recommends $1,000,000 of liability protection.
steps: Check your current home and auto liability limits on existing policies
Ask an insurer for a $1,000,000 umbrella quote to top up liability
Confirm what home and auto cover the umbrella would sit on top of
Compare costs and add the umbrella if it fits your budget

quiz.q: What umbrella liability amount does the plan recommend you consider?
quiz.explain: The plan’s recommended umbrella liability cover is $1,000,000, and you currently have none.

m2.title: Confirm employer 401(k) match
m2.why: Raising retirement saving matters and the plan notes no recorded employer match today.
steps: Contact HR at each employer to ask about 401(k) match details
Find out matching percentage and any vesting rules
If a match exists, adjust payroll deferral to capture it
Revisit how much of your $15,032 free cash to redirect

quiz.q: Why does the plan suggest checking each employer about a 401(k) match?
options: Because no match is recorded today and a match is free return
Because matches replace the need for emergency cash
Because the match will pay off the credit card
quiz.explain: The plan specifically notes no employer match is recorded today and checking for a match helps you capture extra retirement savings.
